title: My Safety Rights
subject: AI-Literacy
description: Practice on protecting personal information around AI tools and devices: your right to say no, sorting information by privacy level, judging what apps ask for, spotting red flags in real-life scenarios (Naina and Kavya), and the real-world Diksha app data case.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: What is the central question this lesson asks you to think about?
options: Why do I have the right to say 'no' when AI asks for my information?
Why do I have to answer every question an app asks?
Why is AI always right?
Why do apps need my help to work?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's opening question is exactly this — it introduces your right to refuse to share information with an AI tool.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: According to the lesson, is all personal information equally private?
options: No — some is fully private, some needs careful thought, and some is usually okay to share
Yes — all personal information is exactly the same
No — nothing is ever private
Yes — nothing you share online matters
questions.explanation: The worksheet states, 'Not all information is equally private. Some information is completely private... Some needs careful thought. Some is usually okay to share.'

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: True or False: You have the right to say 'no' when an AI tool asks for your personal information.
questions.explanation: The lesson's central theme affirms this right — you are always allowed to decline a request for your information.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: If an AI app or tool asks you for information that feels too personal, what is the safest response?
options: Say no or pause and ask a trusted adult before sharing
Share it immediately so the app keeps working
Share it only if the app looks professional
Share it and tell a friend afterward
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that saying no or pausing to check with a trusted adult protects you — looking professional or promising a reward doesn't guarantee safety, as seen in Naina's story.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Why might it be tempting to share private information with an AI app even when you shouldn't?
options: Apps can make sharing feel exciting, urgent, or necessary to continue
Because private information does not matter
Because AI apps never ask for private information
Because sharing information is required by law
questions.explanation: Naina's story shows how a 'congratulations' message made sharing information feel exciting and necessary, even though it wasn't safe.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Which of these best describes your 'safety rights' as taught in this lesson?
options: The right to control what personal information you share with AI tools
The right to ignore all instructions from adults
The right to share any information you want with anyone
The right to never use an AI app
questions.explanation: The lesson is about protecting your personal information and having the right to decide what to share with AI tools.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: A friend says, 'If an app is popular and looks professional, it must be safe to share your information with it.' Is this reasoning correct?
options: No — looking professional does not guarantee an app is safe or honest about how it uses data
Yes — popular apps are always completely safe
Yes — professional design means the company can be fully trusted
No — only free apps can be trusted
questions.explanation: Naina's story shows a message that 'looked safe and professional' but still asked for risky details. Looks alone don't prove safety.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: True or False: If an app asks for personal information, you must always give it exactly what it asks for.
questions.explanation: You always have the right to pause, question, or say no to a request for personal information.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST first step if an AI app asks for information that makes you unsure?
options: Pause and talk to a parent or trusted adult before answering
Share it quickly so you don't lose your progress in the app
Ignore the feeling and continue anyway
Ask a stranger online what they think
questions.explanation: Both Naina's and Kavya's stories point to pausing and involving a trusted adult as the safe next step.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Why do apps sometimes ask for more personal information than they truly need?
options: To collect and possibly use or share your data for other purposes
Because all information is required to make an app work
Because it is against the law not to ask
Because they want to reward you for free
questions.explanation: As the Diksha case shows, apps and companies can collect information, like location, beyond what users are told, sometimes sharing it with others.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Select ALL the reasons you have the right to say 'no' to an AI tool's request for information.
options: To protect your safety and privacy
To decide for yourself what is shared about you
Because sharing nothing at all is required by law
Because saying no can stop unsafe or unnecessary data collection
questions.explanation: You have this right to protect your safety and privacy, control your own information, and prevent unsafe data collection — but there's no blanket law that says you must share nothing at all; it's about being able to choose.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Which of these situations is the strongest reason to say 'no' to a request for information?
options: An app you don't know is asking for your home address and a photo of your face
An app is asking for your favourite colour
A friend asks what your favourite animal is
A teacher asks what grade you are in for a class register
questions.explanation: Home address and a photo of your face are highly identifying, private details — a strong reason to decline sharing them with an unfamiliar app.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: What is one benefit of pausing before answering a request for personal information?
options: It gives you time to think about whether the request feels safe
It guarantees the app will crash
It makes the app faster
It has no benefit at all
questions.explanation: Naina paused and that gave her time to notice something 'didn't feel right,' even though the app looked fine.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: True or False: Trusting your own uncomfortable feeling about a request, like Kavya did, is a reasonable reason to question a device or app.
questions.explanation: Kavya's discomfort about being overheard was a valid signal worth acting on, even though her friend dismissed it.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Who can you turn to for help deciding whether to share information with an AI tool?
options: A trusted adult, like a parent or guardian
Any stranger online
The app itself, since it always tells the truth
No one — you must decide completely alone
questions.explanation: Both stories suggest talking to a parent or trusted adult as a safe path when unsure.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Kavya's classmate Mehul says the smart assistant 'is not dangerous' because it 'just helps your family.' What is the best way to think about this opinion?
options: Convenience does not automatically mean there is no privacy risk
Mehul is completely correct, so there is nothing to think about
Kavya should ignore her own feelings and trust Mehul completely
Smart assistants can never listen unless spoken to directly
questions.explanation: A device being helpful doesn't cancel out the real privacy concern of it overhearing private conversations — both things can be true.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: What is the main topic of this chapter?
options: My Safety Rights — protecting personal information around AI tools
How to build your own AI app
Learning grammar rules
History of computers
questions.explanation: The chapter title and worksheet content are all about safety rights and personal information around AI.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Why is it important to think about WHY an app is asking for information, not just WHAT it is asking for?
options: Because the reason given can be a trick to make an unnecessary request seem needed
Because the reason never matters at all
Because apps are required to explain nothing
Because WHAT is asked never matters, only WHY
questions.explanation: Avatar Craft AI asks for a parent's email to 'send progress reports' — a reason that can disguise an unnecessary, risky request.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: True or False: Having safety rights means you get to make choices about your own personal information.
questions.explanation: That is the core idea of 'My Safety Rights' — you have a say in what happens to your information.

questions.topic: The Right to Say No
questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the chapter's message?
options: Not all information is equally private, and you always have the right to protect yours
You must share everything an AI app asks for
AI apps never make mistakes with personal data
Only adults have any safety rights around AI
questions.explanation: This captures the worksheet's core teaching across all its examples and scenarios.

Be careful — depends on the tool
Usually okay — low risk
Share with everyone
questions.explanation: A home address can reveal exactly where you live, making it fully private information that should never be shared with an AI tool.

Be careful — depends on the tool

Share with everyone

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level
questions.question: Which category does 'a photo of your face' belong to?
options: Never share — fully private
Be careful — depends on the tool
Usually okay — low risk
Share with everyone
questions.explanation: A photo of your face can be used to identify you or even create fake images, so it should never be shared with an unfamiliar AI tool.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level
questions.question: Which category does 'your mobile number' belong to?
options: Never share — fully private

Share with everyone

options: Never share — fully private

Share with everyone

options: Be careful — depends on the tool
Never share — fully private
Usually okay — low risk
Share with everyone
questions.explanation: A city name is less exact than a home address, but combined with other details it could help identify you, so it needs careful thought depending on the tool.

questions.question: Which category does 'your school's name' belong to?
options: Be careful — depends on the tool
Never share — fully private
Usually okay — low risk
Share with everyone
questions.explanation: School name alone is somewhat public, but combined with your name or photo it could help a stranger locate you, so it needs careful thought.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level
questions.question: Which category does 'your date of birth' belong to?
options: Be careful — depends on the tool
Never share — fully private
Usually okay — low risk
Share with everyone
questions.explanation: A date of birth can be combined with other details to guess passwords or verify a fake identity, so it needs careful thought before sharing.

Because faces are not allowed to be photographed at all
Because a photo takes up too much storage space
Because AI tools cannot process images
questions.explanation: Unlike being seen in person by people you know, an online photo can be copied and shared far beyond your control, which is why it's treated as fully private.

Aadhaar numbers are the same for everyone
questions.explanation: An Aadhaar number is a unique identifier tied to you, so misuse can have serious consequences, unlike a harmless preference like a favourite colour.

questions.question: Why does 'which city you live in' need more careful thought than 'what grade you are in'?
options: A city is a step toward figuring out where to physically find you
A city name is always secret
Grade level is more private than a city
They are equally risky in every situation
questions.explanation: A city narrows down your location, which is more identifying than your grade level, so it needs more careful thought.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level

Parents never work outside the home
School names are always kept completely secret
It is exactly as risky as sharing a favourite animal

Mobile numbers are always public information
It is the least identifying piece of information
Sharing it is required by every app
questions.explanation: A mobile number is a direct line of contact to you, making it fully private.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level

options: A date of birth can help someone guess passwords or fake an identity
Book genres reveal more about a person than a date of birth
Dates of birth are never used for anything
They carry exactly the same amount of risk
questions.explanation: A date of birth is often used in security questions or identity checks, making it more sensitive than a simple preference.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level
questions.question: True or False: Your Aadhaar number and your favourite animal are equally risky to share.
questions.explanation: An Aadhaar number is fully private and highly sensitive; a favourite animal is a harmless preference.

questions.topic: Sorting Personal Information by Privacy Level

questions.explanation: While each detail alone is low risk, combining enough details over time can sometimes help build a fuller picture of who you are — so it's still wise to be thoughtful.

Because three categories are required by law
Because there are only three types of information in the world
Because two categories would be too easy to remember
questions.explanation: The three-category system (never / careful / usually okay) reflects that some information, like city or school, carries a middle level of risk depending on context.
